items.title: 68146_Russell Procope oral history interview
items.q: it was very enlightening to sit in the same section with him and see him develop like that

ctx.x: Oh, yes, yes, yes. Well, that was a great thing. Coleman Hawkins was one of the greatest. He was one of the greatest saxophone players because he had such a conception of playing the horn and he was a thorough musician, because he could play all the chords. He knew all the chords, you know, because you can tell just listening to him he played

more actually than anybody else. Of course people have come along since then, but to my mind he did it all. Coleman Hawkins did it all. And it's very interesting to listen to him and his whole career, like the old records he made with Fletcher Henderson, way back when Fletcher first started, which was '23 and '24 and '25, to see Coleman develop, develop as he went along and got older, and it was very enlightening to sit in the same section with him and see him develop like that, you know. Yeah, very -- it was…

learn to play slow then to play fast, but the concentration was on playing fast, like, "Tiger Rag," you know, fast. (Singing). Like that, you know. And the clarinet players were in. The clarinet players -- it's not like now. You don't find clarinet players now.
